headline: Simple Liquid Could Spare Thousands of Children From Dental Surgery
meta_description: FDA approval looms for silver diamine fluoride, a painless cavity treatment that arrests decay without drilling. A major trial proves its safety in young child…
summary_short: A University of Michigan study of 830 children proves silver diamine fluoride safely arrests tooth decay without drilling, shots, or sedation—potentially transforming ca…
body:
Thousands of young American children each year face emergency dental surgery under general anesthesia for untreated cavities. But a University of Michigan-led clinical trial may change that trajectory. Researchers tested silver diamine fluoride (SDF), a simple liquid applied with a tiny sponge-tipped applicator, on 830 children under age 6 across Michigan, New York, and Iowa. The Phase III trial, published in JAMA Pediatrics, found that SDF arrested tooth decay in more than half of affected baby teeth when reapplied every six months—all without drilling, injections, or sedation. The results provide the rigorous evidence needed for FDA approval as a cavity-treatment drug.

Dentists worldwide have used SDF safely for decades, and American practitioners applied it off-label since 2014, when it was approved only for tooth sensitivity. What was missing was large-scale US clinical data. "If we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in US populations, and we now have that," said Margherita Fontana, the study's lead investigator. The treatment works by simply painting the liquid onto the cavity—no removal of tooth structure required. For some children, reapplication every few months until baby teeth naturally fall out may be all that's needed.

The stakes are significant. Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease of childhood, affecting over 40% of US children, often leading to pain, infection, missed school, and repeated medical visits. SDF could be especially valuable for very young children, older adults, people with disabilities, and those with severe dental anxiety who struggle with conventional treatment. The primary drawback is cosmetic: the silver permanently darkens the decayed portion. Still, as researchers note, stopping infection and pain matters most—and this approach could achieve that for nearly anyone who needs it.

Silver diamine fluoride arrests decay without drilling, shots, or sedation
Phase III trial published in JAMA Pediatrics shows over 50% effectiveness
Tooth decay affects more than 40% of US children annually
